To loll means to rest or move in a way that is loose, heavy, and relaxed — without any tension or effort in the body. Think of the way a person sinks deep into a sofa on a lazy Sunday, or the way a dog's tongue hangs out of its mouth on a hot day. That looseness, that giving-in to gravity — that is the essence of loll.

Loll has two usages that are really just two sides of the same coin:

1. A person (or animal) rests in a lazy, drooping, relaxed way

This is when someone's whole body is limp and at ease — slouched, sprawled, or draped somewhere without any uprightness or energy. There is no tension. The body is simply surrendering to the pull of gravity.

  • She lolled in the hammock for hours, not caring about anything.
  • The cat lolled on the warm windowsill in the afternoon sun.
  • He lolled against the wall, half-asleep, waiting for the bus.

2. A body part (especially the tongue or head) hangs loosely

This is when a specific part of the body droops or swings without being held up — usually the tongue, or the head when someone is very tired or unconscious.

  • The dog ran back, its tongue lolling out of its mouth.
  • His head lolled to one side as he dozed off in the chair.
  • The child fell asleep in the car, her head lolling against the window.

Notice how both meanings share the same feeling: no tension, no control, just looseness and gravity doing their work.

Loll is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of idle, unhurried, boneless relaxation. When you say someone is lolling, you are painting a picture of a person who is in no rush whatsoever — whose body has simply let go. Depending on the context, this can feel:

  • Pleasant and peaceful — lolling on a beach, on a holiday, in the sun. There is something indulgent and carefree about it.
  • Lazy or careless — lolling around the house all day while work piles up. Here it can carry a mild sense of criticism.

The word itself does not judge, but the context around it often does.
How Loll Differs From Similar Words

Since loll is close in meaning to several other words, knowing the difference will help you use it precisely.

Loll vs. Lounge — Both describe relaxed resting, but lounge is more neutral and can even feel dignified (a hotel lounge, lounge chairs). Loll is specifically droopier and limper. A person lolling looks less composed than a person lounging.

Loll vs. Slouch — Slouch is specifically about bad posture, often with a negative, disapproving tone (a parent telling a child to stop slouching). Loll is more about the whole body being loose and limp, not necessarily about posture being wrong.

Loll vs. Sprawl — Sprawl suggests spreading out widely and taking up a lot of space, often in a somewhat messy or chaotic way. Loll is more about drooping and hanging loosely — it is not necessarily about space, but about limpness.

Loll vs. Recline — Recline is completely neutral and formal (a reclining seat on a plane). It says nothing about energy or tension. Loll always carries that extra flavour of looseness and ease.

You will most often see loll used in these patterns:

  • Loll + in/on/against/back: loll in the sun, loll on the sofa, loll against a tree, loll back in a chair
  • Loll about/around: meaning to spend time lazily doing nothing — He just lolled about the house all weekend.
  • Body part + loll + out/to one side: tongue lolled out, head lolled to the side
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you ever need a single image to anchor this word in your memory: picture a dog on a hot summer day — panting, tongue hanging out, lying flat on the cool floor without a care in the world. That dog is the very definition of lolling.
